data.title: Pseudo-Macarius: Mysticism and Community
data.abstractNote: In this paper, I will try to explore the social consequences of mystical theology that we can find in Pseudo-Macarius’ works. When we mention Pseudo-Macarius, usually we associate this name with a teaching of prayer that leads to an ascension towards God. However, in my opinion, his understanding of love towards other people and toward God’s creation still remains unexplored. Through his Homilies and his Great Letter, I will try to draw an outline that will show practical implications of his mystical theology upon human relations towards creation and fellow man.

data.title: A Mosaicist’s Workshop in Epiphania (Hama, Syria) at the Beginning of the 5th Century
data.abstractNote: The discovery of numerous mosaics, mostly church pavements, in the region of Hama, ancient Epiphania, northern Syria, in the last forty years, has raised among others the question of their makers: the craftsmen who executed them and their workshop. Although Apamea-on-the-Orontes was a leading center of mosaic production at the turn of the fourth century, it is legitimate to wonder whether an independent workshop, possibly based in Epiphania, concurrently operated to produce these particular mosaics. Three monuments were selected for comparison. Situated north-east of Hama and flanking the ancient roads connecting Antioch to Epiphania, they are the church mosaics of Khirbet Muqa, dated 394/395, Murik and Qumhane, these two attributed to the beginning of the fifth century; Qumhane, in turn, was compared to the cathedral of Epiphania, dated by an inscription to 416 AD. Thus, the probability that the mosaics of Khirbet Muqa, Murik and Qumhane were made by the same workshop is consolidated, not only by the internal criteria used to identify a workshop, but also by an external criterion : that of sufficient demand and the financial means to provide for it: in this particular instance, the socio-economic context of pilgrimage to the Holy Land.

data.title: Pseudo-Clementine ‘Recognitions’ 1.27-71: Early Jewish Christian Perspectives on the Nature and History of Christianity
data.abstractNote: The Pseudo-Clementine Recognitions 1.27-71 are examined here as a source for early Jewish Christian perspectives on the nature and history of Christianity. Chapter 1 reviews previous scholarship and thereby discloses possibilities for interpretation. Though one scholar’s position has become dominant in modern times, it has not been thoroughly examined. Furthermore, the Syriac translation of the text has been neglected in favor of Rufinus’s Latin rendering. Chapter 2 addresses this problem of evaluating the two extant ancient translations of the lost Greek Recognitions. Rufinus’s theory of translation and his comments on his rendering of the Pseudo-Clementines are investigated. Recently discovered Armenian fragments and other acknowledged criteria reveal that while each of the two translations has its own peculiar shortcomings, they are of approximately the same accuracy.  Chapter 3 provides the first modern complete translation of the Syriac of Recognitions 1.27-71. Chapter 4 addresses the widely held thesis that this material is based on a special source. The literary place of this passage in the Recognitions and in the lost basic writing is identified, and the redaction of each author is isolated. Since the views of the remaining material differ from what is elsewhere attributable to the basic writing, this material seems indeed to derive from a special source. The limits of this source are identified as Recognitions 1.27.1-44.1, 53.4-71.6. Examination of this material reveals that its author, writing under the name of Matthew, employed the Greek Old Testament, the Book of Jubilees, Matthew, Luke, Acts, Hegesippus, Justin, and possibly the Gospel of the Ebionites. While some Jewish Christian themes are shared with the Anabathmoi Jakobou, evidence for dependency on this writing is insufficient. Chapter 5 concludes that the author is a Jewish Christian of about 200 C.E. He values astrology, sees Christianity as true Judaism, and is concerned with the Christian inheritance of the land of Israel. He possibly writes as a Jewish Christian presbyter or bishop in Jerusalem or Judaea.
